summary: The SIP REFER method automatically sets up a short-lived subscription so the sender hears about progress. Those notifications are not always wanted. This document adds a header field in a REFER request to prevent that subscription. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: When you ask a friend to make a call for you, they normally keep telling you how it is going. This lets you say no updates needed.

questions: what is the sip refer-sub header
how to stop refer notifications in sip
can a refer be sent without a subscription
subtitle: A SIP header that lets the sender of a REFER say it does not want the automatic subscription and its notifications.

tldr.problem: Every SIP REFER automatically creates an implicit subscription, and at least one NOTIFY is sent back. That is wasted traffic when the sender does not need progress reports, for example when it already follows the dialog event package.
tldr.mechanism: The sender adds a Refer-Sub header set to false. If the recipient agrees, it echoes Refer-Sub: false in its 2xx response and creates no subscription or dialog. A new option tag, norefersub, signals support.
tldr.outcome: REFER can be used without subscription overhead, but only when the sender is sure the request will not fork.

today: RFC 4488 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It extends the REFER method of RFC 3515.

sections.title: Why Suppress the Subscription
sections.content:
The REFER specification (RFC 3515) requires every REFER to create an implicit subscription between the REFER-Issuer and the REFER-Recipient. This results in at least one NOTIFY sent from the recipient to the issuer. The recipient may cancel the subscription with that NOTIFY, or the issuer may cancel it with a SUBSCRIBE carrying Expires: 0.

The subscription has two purposes. First, it lets the issuer see the multiple dialogs that a forked REFER could create, the same approach used for forked SUBSCRIBE requests. If the issuer states that forking must not occur, that need disappears. Second, the NOTIFY reports progress of the resulting transaction. If the issuer already knows the progress, for example through an explicit subscription to the dialog event package at the recipient, the extra NOTIFY traffic is unnecessary network overhead.
sections.eli5: Normally, when you ask someone to do a job, they report back. If you are already watching them work, the reports are just noise.

sections.title: Roles and the New Tokens
sections.content:
The RFC uses three terms. The REFER-Issuer is the UA sending the REFER. The REFER-Recipient is the UA receiving it. The REFER-Target is the UA named in the Refer-To URI.

It defines a new header field, Refer-Sub, which is meaningful only within a REFER transaction. Set to false, it asks the recipient not to establish an implicit subscription and the resulting dialog. It also defines a new option tag, norefersub, which a UA places in the Supported header field to say it can accept a REFER without creating an implicit subscription.
sections.eli5: There is the person asking, the person doing the asking-for, and the person to be called. A new word, Refer-Sub, lets the asker say 'no reports please'.

sections.title: The Refer-Sub Header
sections.content:
Refer-Sub MAY be used only with a REFER request and the matching 2xx response. It may be encrypted as part of end-to-end encryption. The syntax is Refer-Sub = "Refer-Sub" HCOLON refer-sub-value *(SEMI exten), where the value is true or false and exten is a generic parameter.

Even with the extension in use, the REFER remains a target refresh request, as it does by default.

The RFC also adds a courtesy row for the header to the SIP header table: it applies to requests (R) and 2xx responses, and is optional (o) in REFER.
sections.eli5: The header is a small sticky note on the request that says 'true' or 'false' for whether you want reports.

sections.title: How the Exchange Works
sections.content:
The issuer adds Refer-Sub: false to the REFER. If the recipient supports the extension and is willing to proceed without a subscription, it MUST insert Refer-Sub: false in its 2xx response. No implicit subscription is created, and no new dialog is created if the REFER was issued outside an existing dialog.

If the recipient does not include the header, or includes it set to true, the implicit subscription is created as usual. So the header is a request that the recipient can decline.

The issuer can learn support from the Supported header field of the dialog-initiating request or response, or through presence. Using Require: norefersub when capabilities are unknown is NOT RECOMMENDED, because an unsupporting recipient rejects the request with a 420 (Bad Extension) response and the issuer needs another round trip to fall back to a normal REFER. Require: norefersub can appear together with Refer-Sub: false.
sections.eli5: You ask 'no reports, please'. The helper says 'okay, no reports' by repeating it, or stays quiet and reports anyway.

sections.title: Forking and the Example
sections.content:
A REFER sent outside an existing dialog can fork, and a proxy may fork an unknown method. If forking happens, the issuer will not notice, because the forking proxy forwards only a single 2xx response. So the issuer is responsible for making sure no forking will result.

If a REFER to a Request-URI might fork, the issuer SHOULD NOT include Refer-Sub. It SHOULD use standardized mechanisms to prevent forking. Absent any other mechanism, the Request-URI SHOULD have GRUU properties, which ensure the request will not fork.

The RFC's example is a REFER with Refer-To: <sip:c@example.com;method=INVITE>, Refer-Sub: false and Supported: norefersub.
sections.eli5: If your message might go to several people at once, you cannot skip the reports, because you would not know which one answered.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
A malicious Refer-Sub: false reduces the processing and state needed at the recipient, so the RFC sees limited use in denial-of-service attacks. A man in the middle, however, could add the header to suppress notifications without the issuer noticing, or remove it so the recipient generates notifications the issuer had suppressed. The RFC says integrity protection should be used, for example S/MIME as discussed in RFC 3261.

IANA registers the Refer-Sub header field (no compact form) and the norefersub option tag.
sections.eli5: Someone sneaky could add or erase the 'no reports' note, so the message should be sealed against tampering.

data.title: REFER with Refer-Sub: false
data.code:
REFER sip:pc-b@example.com SIP/2.0
Via: SIP/2.0/TCP issuer.example.com;branch=z9hG4bK-a-1
From: <sip:a@example.com>;tag=1a
Call-ID: 1@issuer.example.com
CSeq: 234234 REFER
Max-Forwards: 70
Refer-To: <sip:c@example.com;method=INVITE>
Refer-Sub: false
Supported: norefersub
Contact: sip:a@issuer.example.com
Content-Length: 0

left.title: REFER with Refer-Sub: false
left.desc: Asks that no implicit subscription be created.

right.title: 2xx with Refer-Sub: false
right.desc: Grants it: no subscription and no new dialog.
